overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of what happens to information you give an AI tool and what rights attach to what it produces. You'll be asked about retention, review, and training use; consumer, business, and local arrangements; categories of information to keep out of a prompt; and the human authorship requirement in US copyright law.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: You switch off the setting that lets a provider use your conversations to train its models. What does that change, going by what providers' own pages describe?

options.html: Your conversations are no longer stored by the provider
options.text: Your conversations are no longer stored by the provider
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Retention is separate from training use. Switching off training stops that one use, and conversations may still be kept and in some cases reviewed.

options.html: No person at the provider can ever read your conversations
options.text: No person at the provider can ever read your conversations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Human review is separate from training use. Switching off training stops that one use, and conversations may still be kept and in some cases reviewed.

options.html: Training use stops, and retention may still continue
options.text: Training use stops, and retention may still continue
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Retention, human review, and training use are separate. A training setting answers one of the three questions and may leave the other two as they were.

options.html: Your past conversations are deleted from the provider's systems
options.text: Your past conversations are deleted from the provider's systems
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A training setting doesn't delete anything. It stops that one use, and conversations may still be kept and in some cases reviewed.

forms.stemHtml: A project manager pays for a personal subscription to an AI assistant. Her employer licenses a different assistant for staff. Which statement describes her personal subscription?

options.html: It's a consumer account under the provider's standard terms
options.text: It's a consumer account under the provider's standard terms
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! An account an individual opens directly with a provider is a consumer account, whether free or paid. Her employer hasn't agreed to its terms.

options.html: It's a work tool, because she uses it during her working hours
options.text: It's a work tool, because she uses it during her working hours
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. When she uses it doesn't change the arrangement. An account she opened herself is a consumer account under the provider's standard terms.

options.html: It comes under enterprise terms, because she pays a monthly fee
options.text: It comes under enterprise terms, because she pays a monthly fee
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Paying doesn't make a personal account an organizational one. An account she opened herself is a consumer account under the provider's standard terms.

options.html: It's a local deployment, because the app runs on her own laptop
options.text: It's a local deployment, because the app runs on her own laptop
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Local deployment means the model itself runs on her machine. Her text still goes to the provider, and her account is a consumer account under the provider's standard terms.

forms.stemHtml: Which of these should stay out of an AI tool unless a rule you're bound by permits it? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: A colleague's performance review
options.text: A colleague's performance review
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is another person's personal information, and usually confidential to the employer as well.

options.html: A client's unreleased financial results
options.text: A client's unreleased financial results
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is confidential client material.

options.html: A named student's grades and accommodation notes
options.text: A named student's grades and accommodation notes
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! These are student records. In the United States they come under FERPA, and the school decides which services may receive them.

options.html: A draft agenda you wrote for a public event
options.text: A draft agenda you wrote for a public event
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Your own draft about a public event involves nobody else's information. The categories to keep out are other people's personal details, confidential client and employer material, health and financial information, and student records.

forms.stemHtml: A teacher wants help wording feedback for a student. Which approach is an example of de-identification?

options.html: Pasting the student's work and asking the tool to keep it private
options.text: Pasting the student's work and asking the tool to keep it private
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Asking a tool to keep something private doesn't change what was sent. De-identification means removing or replacing the details that would show who the material is about.

options.html: Using a personal account in place of the school's approved tool
options.text: Using a personal account in place of the school's approved tool
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Changing accounts doesn't alter the material, and a personal account hasn't been reviewed by the school. De-identification means removing or replacing the details that would show who the material is about.

options.html: Deleting the conversation as soon as the feedback is written
options.text: Deleting the conversation as soon as the feedback is written
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Deleting afterward doesn't change what was sent. De-identification means removing or replacing the details that would show who the material is about.

options.html: Describing the work in general terms with no name or details
options.text: Describing the work in general terms with no name or details
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! De-identification removes or replaces the details that would let someone work out who the material is about, and it takes more than deleting the name.

forms.stemHtml: Under the US Copyright Office's 2025 report, which of these falls outside copyright protection?

options.html: An essay you wrote and then had an AI tool check for grammar
options.text: An essay you wrote and then had an AI tool check for grammar
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The Office says using AI to assist your own writing doesn't affect your protection. What falls outside protection is material generated entirely by AI from a prompt.

options.html: An image an AI system generated from your one-line prompt
options.text: An image an AI system generated from your one-line prompt
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The report says copyright doesn't extend to purely AI-generated material and that prompts alone don't give enough human control to make the user the author.

options.html: Your creative arrangement of several AI-generated passages
options.text: Your creative arrangement of several AI-generated passages
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The Office says a person's creative selection and arrangement of AI material can be protected. What falls outside protection is material generated entirely by AI from a prompt.

options.html: A report you drafted yourself after brainstorming with a chatbot
options.text: A report you drafted yourself after brainstorming with a chatbot
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A report you wrote is your own expression. What falls outside protection is material generated entirely by AI from a prompt.

title: Privacy, confidentiality, and copyright in your own use
